sentences.text: 2. It is submitted by learned counsel for the petitioner that the acquisition of petitioner's land is dehors the provisions of National Highways Act, 1956 (for short "Act of 1956") and against the respondent's own documents; marked as Annexure-19 and Annexure-21.
The purpose of acquiring the land was for expansion of the highway, whereas the land of the petitioner is situated at a far away place and is/was not used for the proposed highway extension.
Learned counsel further submits that the land is still lying vacant after all these years and the physical possession of the land is also with the petitioner.
3. Per contra, learned counsel for the respondents have submitted that it is undisputed that the acquisition proceedings were duly carried out in accordance with law.

Learned counsel for the respondents have relied upon the definition of 'highway' as provided under Section 4 of the Act of 1956 to submit that the definition of highway is broad enough to include the land of the petitioner as well.

Learned counsel for the respondents have also brought attention of this Court to the contents of the Additional Affidavit filed on behalf of Respondent No. 2 to submit that due to compelling and specific reasons, the land of the petitioner was [2023/RJJP/010745] (3 of 4) [CW-17149/2010]
acquired.
It is stated that the land was acquired keeping in view of the Indian Road Congress Guidelines, 1980 and to accommodate various legal, technical and structural requirements.

Learned counsel for the respondents further contends that it is immaterial whether the petitioner claims to be in physical possession of the land in question as after conclusion of land acquisition proceedings,
the land vests with the State and if the petitioner is still occupying the said land then he would be occupying it as an illegal encroacher.

4. In rejoinder, learned counsel for the petitioner again reiterated that the land of the petitioner is situated at a considerable distance from the highway and even after expansion of highway, the land of the petitioner is still far enough so as to not be included in the definition of 'highway', as per the Act of 1956.
5. Heard and considered.
6.
On perusal of the record of the case, especially the additional affidavit, it is noted that sufficient reasons are made out by the respondents for acquisition of the land in question.
It is also noted that the respondents have duly released the amount of compensation in favour of the petitioner.

However, considering that the writ petition contains some hotly disputed questions of facts, which are highly technical in nature, this Court grants liberty to the petitioner to file representation before competent authority of respondent no. 2.
The said representation be filed within a period of two weeks.
The respondent no

. 2 is directed to consider the representation of petitioner,

2 weeks and pass a reasoned order in accordance with law.
